  against the cloud, and then he took it up to the kitchen and cut the string with the knife he used for the bread.

  Inside was a tin of the peppermint sweets that Ada had always kept in her apron pocket, and a card. The card said:
  Dad. I heard. I am sorry. I am coming out before the end of the season if the boat will take me. Lise. And under that,
  in different ink, as though it had been written later and added as an afterthought: Keep the log going. Please.

  Walter sat with the card for a long time. Then he took a pen and wrote in the log, in the column for remarks, Supply
  boat in. Post received. It was the first entry he had made in a week that was not a reading. He looked at it for a
  while and then added, Daughter coming out, weather permitting.

  ---

  April was mild, and then May was wet, and June came in with long light evenings that made the lamp seem almost
  foolish. The fishing boats from the harbour came out past the rock in greater numbers, and Walter took to counting
  them. Forty-one in one day. He wrote the number down. He wrote down the weather and the sea state and the visibility,
  which was always good, because he was the sort of man who wrote things down whether or not anyone would ever read
  them.

  Lise did not come in June. The boat was full of cement and new winches for the harbour master's office, and Declan
  said there would
